Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases and Pr: Gases are described by the kinetic molecular theory: gas particles are very small compared with the distances between them, move randomly in straight lines, collide elastically and have no attractions. The average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature. Gas pressure is caused by collisions with the walls. Pressure units: 1 atm = 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg = 760 torr. Temperature must be in kelvins, K = C + 273. Standard temperature and pressure (STP) is 273 K and 1 atm. Real gases behave ideally at high temperature and low pressure.
Boyle's, Charles's and Gay-Lussac's Laws: For a fixed amount of gas the three simple laws are: Boyle's law (constant temperature) P1 V1 = P2 V2, so pressure and volume are inversely proportional; Charles's law (constant pressure) V1 / T1 = V2 / T2, so volume is proportional to the absolute temperature; Gay-Lussac's law (constant volume) P1 / T1 = P2 / T2. They combine into P1 V1 / T1 = P2 V2 / T2. Temperatures must be in kelvins, and the pressure and volume units only need to be the same on both sides. Compressing a gas at constant temperature raises its pressure, and heating a rigid container raises its pressure.
The Ideal Gas Law: The ideal gas law combines all gas relationships: PV = nRT. With pressure in atm and volume in liters, R = 0.0821 L atm/(mol K); with pressure in pascals and volume in cubic meters, R = 8.31 J/(mol K). It lets you find any one of P, V, n and T when the others are known. The molar mass of a gas can be found from M = m R T / (P V), and the density from d = P M / (R T). At STP one mole occupies 22.4 L. The combined gas law follows from the ideal gas law when n is constant.
Dalton's Law, Gas Mixtures and Gas Stoic: In a mixture of gases that do not react, each gas exerts a partial pressure as if it were alone, and the total pressure is the sum: P_total = P1 + P2 + P3 + ... (Dalton's law). The partial pressure of a gas is P_i = X_i P_total, where X_i = n_i / n_total is its mole fraction. Gases collected over water are mixed with water vapor, so P_gas = P_total - P_water vapor. Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes: gases react in simple whole-number volume ratios at the same T and P, the same as the coefficients. Gas stoichiometry uses PV = nRT to convert between moles and volume at the given conditions.
Diffusion, Effusion and Real Gases: Diffusion is the spreading of gas particles to fill the available space, and effusion is the escape of a gas through a tiny hole. Graham's law says that the rate is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass: rate1 / rate2 = sqrt(M2 / M1). Lighter gases such as hydrogen move faster than heavier gases. The root-mean-square speed is v = sqrt(3RT / M) with M in kg/mol and R = 8.31. Real gases deviate from ideal behavior at high pressure (particle volume matters) and low temperature (attractions matter); the van der Waals equation corrects PV = nRT for these effects. A gas liquefies when cooled enough, and below the critical temperature it can be liquefied by pressure.
